Introduction to Coding & Programming

Model:  All

Production:  All

After completion of this module you will be able to:

• Distinguish between Coding & Programming

• Understand the importance of Coding & Programming

• Understand where data is stored in a Control Module



What is Coding?

It is a process utilized by BMW, which groups system specific operating requirements
(Data) together and then assigns a label/code to each of these groups of data.  The vari-
ous groups of data are all pre-loaded into system specific “codable” control modules,
along with a basic set of operating instructions (Program).

Types of operating requirements:

• Nominal values of device input signals (0.25V to 2.5V, 5W - 25W, ...)

• Type of device input signal (PWM, square wave, analog ...)

• Operational parameters (device activation/deactivation time, ...)

• Market specific operations (O2 Sensors, Fuel Type, Emission Control, ...)

• Country Specific Regulations (U.S., Canada, Japan, UK, ECE, ...)

• Powertrain Configurations (Manual, Auto, TLEV, ULEV, SULEV, Diesel, ...)

The procedure of assigning one specifically labeled group of data to the operating pro-
gram of a specific control module/component is referred to as “coding”.

A “codable” control module has a basic operating program already installed along with
several specific variations of operating data.  The coding process allows a specific set of
operating data to be assigned to the basic operating program of that module/component,
with respect to its specific application.

Coding can be performed for some systems/components:

• By installing a specific plug (coding plug) into a device/component

• By entering a 4 digit alpha-numeric code (variant code) via the programming selec-
tion on DISplus/GT1/SSS

• Selecting customer specific system operational settings from a list of available fea-
tures (VKM)

• Automatically by selecting a specific coding process available via ZCS Coding or CIP
using the DISplus/GT1/SSS

Note: Codable control modules/components are system specific, which means
that not all control modules are codable.

What is Programming?

It is a process utilized by BMW to load application/system specific operating instructions

(Program) into a module/component which already has the systems operating require-
ments (Data) installed, plus it can be used as a means of updating data and operating
instructions previously installed in a control module.

Basic programmable control modules have a pre-defined set of operating data already
installed which allows the module to be fairly generic until a specific operational program
is installed.

Programming of system control modules is performed using a DISplus/GT1/SSS.

Note: Programmable control modules are system specific and not all control
modules are programmable using workshop equipment like the
DISplus,GT1 or SSS.  The ability to program a module is limited to the
number of times it has already been programmed and the hardware
version of the control module itself.

What is the Purpose of Coding and Programming?

As a global manufacturer, BMW must design a large variety of control modules to meet
numerous vehicle requirements pertaining to issues such as:

• Country Specific Regulations (U.S., Canada, Japan, UK, ECE, ...)

• Vehicle Equipment Level (Phone, Navigation, HiFi, IHKA, IHKR, ...)

• Vehicle Powertrain Configurations (Manual, Auto, TLEV, ULEV, SULEV, Diesel, ...)

• System Specific Operating Requirements (Nominal values, type of input signal, ...)

By using Coding and/or Programming, the large variety of control modules needed can be
reduced to a smaller number of model specific hardware variations.

Codable control modules contain:

• A common operating program

• A large number/variety of specific operating data groups

In order to use this type of control module it must first be CODED to ensure that the
operating data specific to that vehicle/model application is used by the operating program
of the control module.

Programmable control modules contain:

• The required/specific operational data

• No operating program

In order to use this type of control module it must first be PROGRAMMED to ensure that
the operating program specific to the vehicle/model application is used.

Prior to the availability of Coding and Programming in the workshop this task could only
be performed at the factory.  

Initially the factory installed Control Module(s) with a common operating program or data
into vehicles and as theses vehicles reached various points in the assembly process the
control modules were updated with the required operating data or program specific to the
application for that particular vehicle.  Since replacement parts always need to be avail-
able, parts inventory needed to contain all variations of preprogrammed control modules
installed in all varieties of vehicles that were manufactured.  This was not a big problem in
the early years, when the variety/quantity of models was smaller.

5
Introduction to Coding & Programming



As the number of control modules and the complexity of the various systems installed
into vehicles increased, the number of modules that needed to be stored in parts invento-
ry began to increase as well.  Eventually this led to the stocking of hundreds of different
control modules that were either pre-programmed or pre-coded for a specific application
and model, but only differed slightly in the way they were coded or programmed.

Pre-programmed and pre-coded control modules always needed to be available in the
event a control module failed once the vehicle left the factory floor, since this was the only
place programming & coding procedures could be performed.  In order for repairs to be
made quickly, dealers were required to maintain a stock of several varieties of control
modules, since technicians could only remove the failed module and installed a new pre-
programmed or pre-coded module into the vehicle.

As a result of having to maintain a very large inventory of pre-programmed and pre-coded
control modules in parts inventory, it was decided to make coding and eventually pro-
gramming available in BMW workshops.

The following advantages have occurred since programming and coding can be per-
formed in the workshop:

• Fewer control module hardware versions are needed (only need basic control mod-
ules)

• Lower parts and inventory costs

• Able to update software in a control module without having to replace the module
(Re-Code/ Re-Program to address service Measures)

• Ability to add special equipment features to existing control modules (DWA, Day
Time  Running Lights, ...)

• Customization of vehicle operation (Conversions, VKM, A/C, ...)

6
Introduction to Coding & Programming

DME



The means by which coding or programming information is provided to a control module
varies and is determined by the vehicle, model year and type of module(s) installed.

BMW currently uses the following methods to perform Coding or Programming:

• Coding Plug

• DME variant Coding

• Coding Code

• Central Coding Key (ZCS) or Vehicle Order (VO)

• EPROM Programming

• Flash Programming

• Vehicle and Key Memory (VKM)

Where is Data Stored in a Control Module?

The control modules used in our vehicles store data/information on one of the following:

• EPROM (Electrically Programmable Read Only Memory)

• EEPROM (Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory)

In essence these devices are similar to the harddrive of the PC (Personal Computer) that
many of us use daily to store the images and documents/files of information.

EPROM (Electrically Programmable Read Only Memory)

An EPROM is a computer memory chip that can be electrically programmed, however in
order to erase data that is stored on the chip it must be removed from the device and
exposed to UV lighting for a specific time period.  An EPROM has what is commonly
called a “window” on the top portion of the chip usually located underneath a protective
label, it is this area that must be exposed to UV light of a certain intensity for a specific
time period in order to erase the information stored on it.

Early engine control modules (DME 3.X) and transmission control modules were the first
devices which allowed technicians to first remove the chip from the module, install a new
“blank” EPROM and then program the module.

DMEDME



8
Introduction to Coding & Programming

EEPROM (Electrically Programmable Read Only Memory)

An EEPROM is a computer memory chip that can be electrically programmed and elec-
trically erased, thereby not requiring the chip to be removed from the module or exposed
to light.  In general this chip is not easily removable from the device it is installed into.

Since the entire process of programming and erasing is done electronically this device is
commonly referred to as “Flash Programmable”.

During the programming process the following type of information may be loaded into the
control module depending on the specific application or update that needs to be
installed:

• Characteristic Maps (Ex. Ignition, Injection, Purge Control, DSC Regulation, ...)

• Control Constants/ Operational Data

• Operational Program

• Control Module Identification Information (Ex. Hardware Number, Program Number,
Date of Modification, ...)

What is needed to Code and Program?

In order to code or program a vehicle or control in the workshop, specific equipment and
special software is required such as a DISplus, GT1 and an SSS which must all be con-
nected to a network and have the must current version of CIP (Coding, Individualization &
Programming) installed.  CIP is the software program that contains all the latest data and
program information to allow control modules to be updated to the latest level to address
customer concerns and implement service solutions.

With the release of CIP 15.0 and the implementation of Progman (see Progman section
for additional information) the DISplus and GT1 will only be capable of performing vehicle
diagnosis and activation/initiation of a Coding, Individualization or Programming task
through the SSS.  A special program management tool (Progman) will only allow the
DISplus and GT1 to act as remote terminals to the SSS (regarding Coding,
Individualization & Programming), which means that the SSS will be the single supplier of
Coding, Individualization and Programming information to a vehicle and its respective
control modules.

Networks

As the level of technology in our vehicles continues to increase so does the level of tech-
nology that we use in our diagnostic and programming equipment within the workshop.

In order to meet the ever growing demand for more rapid transfer of information we can
no longer have multiple “stand alone” systems, therefore various infrastructures have
been created to allow multiple “stand alone” devices/systems to interact with each other
to share information.

The sharing of information with various control modules in our vehicles has been occur-
ring for quite some time, now we will also be doing this with the diagnostic equipment in
the workshop as well.

Vehicle Bus Systems

In order to make the components used in our
vehicles more efficient we utilize bus struc-
tures (commonly referred to as I-Bus, K-Bus,
MOST Bus, Byteflight, PT-CAN, etc.).  By
using bus structures in vehicles, we can
accelerate communication between several
different control modules.  Many common
vehicle systems (such as entertainment, safe-
ty, powertrain, etc.) are “stand alone” systems
but also require information from other mod-
ules/systems in order to be more efficient.  In
order to obtain the required information the
systems must also be able to simultaneously
communicate without interfering with each
other, which is accomplished by using various
bus structures.

Example:
The ISIS (Intelligent Safety Integration
System) system on the E65 uses the
Byteflight bus structure.

Depending on the equipment level of the E65, the ISIS may consist of 11 satellite com-
ponents (Control Modules/Sensors) that are connected, using fiberoptic cables, to the
SIM (Safety Information Module) which monitors the status of the satellite components.
Since this is a safety system, components need to be activated within a fraction of a sec-
ond in order to be effective, there can not be any processing delays.  The SIM is con-
nected to the ZGM (Central Gateway Module) which monitors the activity of the SIM and
will direct information to the SIM and other devices in the vehicles as necessary.

Workshop LAN Network

A network is nothing more than a group of devices interconnected so that they can com-
municate with each other.  A LAN is a network that is localized to a specific area, such as
a workshop or office.

The bus systems (I-Bus, K-Bus, PT-CAN, Byteflight, MOST Bus, ...) that we have been
using in our vehicles for quite sometime, are nothing more than networks with different
configurations.  By looking at the byteflight system mentioned previously, a similarity to a
workshop network can be established.

All workshops are currently equipped with a GT1, DISplus, SSS, OPS, OPPS, Diagnostic
Head, Access Point, desktop computer(s) and printer(s) which can be considered as
satellite components (control modules/sensors).  In order for these components to com-
municate with each other, either directly or indirectly, they must be interconnected via a
cable/wire to a common point or switching device.  Consider the switching device/hub to
be similar to the SIM, which monitors all devices connected to it and allows the devices
to communicate with each other.  The interconnection of these devices results in the
establishment of a network localized to the workshop area thereby establishing a Local
Area Network (LAN) in the workshop.

Network Structure

By having the workshop configured to allow the various devices used on a daily basis to
be interconnected/networked with each other, as indicated in the illustration, additional
components can easily be added and online updates can automatically be installed on all
connected devices, as long as they have an approved IP address.

Example:  The network that exist in the workshop is not much different than the net-
work structure that is used in our vehicles.  In order for control modules to
communicate with each other they must be correctly identified.  The identifi-
cation process can be considered to occur as part of the coding procedure
which is done at the end of the assembly process or at anytime a new com-
ponent/module/system is added to the vehicle.  By not recoding the vehicle
after adding or removing a module/system, the communication on a particular
bus can be hampered especially if a response form a module that is no
longer installed is expected or a new module transmits data that is not
expected by anyone else on the bus because it is not correctly identified.
The VO for a vehicle can be considered to contain the IP addresses of the
modules installed in the vehicle.

If the devices on the workshop network do not have a rigidly assigned IP address, online
updates to specific devices can not occur.  The operation/performance of a network can
be greatly hampered if multiple devices share an address, since the transmitted data is
not able to reach the correct device, it can result in jamming up the operation of the net-
work.

Common Terminology

Network
A group of computers that are interconnected with each other and able to communicate
with each other either by transferring data via a wired or wireless connection.

Local Area Network (LAN)
A network that exists within a specific area.

Example: By having all computers, testers and printers in the workshop
interconnected results in a Workshop LAN.

Ethernet
The term Ethernet is a communications protocol used to define a method & speed by
which interconnected devices are able to communicate with each other by either a wired
(twisted pair) or fiberoptic connection.  

Common Ethernet communication protocol terms:

10BaseT - Able to transmit data at a rate of 10Mbps for a maximum distance of
100 meters per segment.

100BaseT - Able to transmit data at a rate of 100Mbps for a maximum distance of
1000 meters per segment.

The speed differences are obtained by modifying the method of encoding the data to be
transferred. The maximum distance consist of the distance from switched hub to wall jack
plus length of cable used to connect a particular device.  The greater the distance the
greater the chance of signal loss/disturbance.

Ethernet Cable (CAT 5)
A standard used to define an 8 wire cable (4 twisted pair) that is commonly used to inter-
connect various computers in the establishment of an ethernet network.  Certified to
transmit data at a maximum rate of 100Mbps.

RJ-45 Connectors
The plastic connectors at the end of a CAT 5 cable, used to connect the cable to
device/computer, wall jack and hub.

Wall Jack
Accepts RJ-45 connectors when connecting devices to the network.  Connection point
for devices like DISplus, GT1, SSS, OPPS, OPS, Diagnostic Head, workshop computers
and printer.  

Recommendation is that outlet/jack is numbered and the corresponding end of the ether-
net cable connected to the switched hub is numbered as well, to assist in troubleshoot-
ing in the event of a problem.

Example: A wall jack outlet is labeled as #1 the other end of the cable at the hub
should also be labeled #1.



20
Coding & Programming Equipment

Switched HUB
Allows multiple devices to send information over the network at the same time without
slowing down the communication process.  A switched hub essentially isolates the two
devices that are communicating, thereby providing each component on the network a
separate connection at the maximum data transfer rate of the network.  

Example: A switched HUB is similar to the use of cloverleafs on the highway, traffic
does not need to stop if a change in direction needs to be made, plus traffic
flows smoothly from point to point.

A regular HUB does not provide each component with a separate connection point to the
network but rather a shared connection point.  By sharing a connection point the data
transfer rate of the network is reduced when multiple devices try to communicate.

Example: A regular HUB is similar to the use of a 4 way intersection, the smaller the
amount of traffic using the intersection the quicker a car can go through the
intersection and reach its desired destination.  The greater the traffic the
longer it will take for a car to reach its desired destination.

The switched hub installed as part of the workshop wiring project is a Cisco WS-C2950-
24.

Network Server
A computer that provides information/data to other computers located on the network.  A
server allows computers on its network to access information on another network, such
as the internet.  The server is the keystone device that allows computers on its specific
network to access information on another network.

As an example a server can obtain and distribute software updates to all computers locat-
ed on its network, instead of having to physically install the updates to each computer
individually.

Automatic/Online Updates
The ability to connect the network server to the BMW server and check for new software
updates (Diagnostic, Coding & Programming data) then downloads the information to all
computers/equipment located on the network automatically at a specific time.

Example: New updates can be installed on SSS, GT1 and DISplus overnight in order to
have latest data available the next morning.

The application that performs online updates is referred to as JETstream.

Access Point
The access point is a wireless communication device that is able to establish a wireless
connection with a GT1 and/or a diagnostic head and allows them to communicate with
other devices on the network.

Manufactured by Symbol - Model Spectrum 24 /AP 3020-100.



21
Coding & Programming Equipment

Interface Name
The specific name assigned to the device (Ex. OPS Blue A)

IP Address
It is a unique four segment number used to identify a specific device located on a specific
network.  The number represents the address of the device on the network and is neces-
sary when communicating with other devices located on the network.

Example: 92.168.100.10
Usually the first three segments are used to identify the network and the last
segment identifies the device.  The IP Subnet Mask information generally
defines which segments are needed to identify the network and which identi-
fy the device.

In order for a devices on the network to communicate with other devices on the network
it must know the addresses of those devices.  If a print command is sent from a computer
to a printer on the network, the command must be addressed specifically to the desired
printer.

Example: An IP address is no different than your home address, in order to receive a
letter specifically directed to you, your name and address must be correctly
displayed on the letter.

IP addresses are assigned by the network administrator/provider and are rigidly assigned
to the device(s) located within the workshop network, by entering it into the device during
the initial setup.

IP Subnet Mask
This information is used to define which segment(s) of the four segment IP address
specifically identifies the device and which identify the specific network.

Example: 255.255.255.0
Indicates that the first three segments (255.255.255) identify the specific
network that the device is located on.  The last segment (0) indicates that
this is the segment that will identify the specific device.



22
Coding & Programming Equipment

Gateway
This information identifies the four segment address of the component located on the
network responsible for communicating from the current network to another network.  If
there is no address in this location then a connection to any devices outside of the cur-
rent network can not be established.

Note: The network and device address information must be entered exactly as
defined by the network administrator for your facility, otherwise the

Procedure for Coding & Programming

An important prerequisite for ensuring trouble-free programming is the correct prepara-
tion of the vehicle. 

A diagnostic procedure must first be performed on the vehicle prior to any pro-
gramming.  Programming must not be started before faults in the vehicle elec-
trical system are ruled out.

Correct preparation of the vehicle avoids errors during programming.

The programming procedure may be terminated if a bus signal is generated as the result
of activation of electric loads during programming.  The programming procedure should
be repeated following termination.  In exceptional cases it may be necessary to replace
the control unit if communication is no longer possible.

Prior to beginning any programming or coding procedure some general guidelines need
to be considered in order to ensure that the process goes as smoothly as possible:

Check Action/Procedure

- System temperature below 80°C.

electromechanical parking brake.

Loads
- All electric loads, lights and indicator lights switched off.
- Wipe/wash system switched off. Insure that the wipers can move freely.

Coding Plug

A coding plug is a mechanically keyed or electronically coded device/plug, that can open
or bridge circuits in a particular component to allow it to operate differently dependent on
the type of plug installed/inserted.

BMW used a mechanical coding plug which simply opened
or bridged circuits to assign market specific data to the
instrument cluster of the E23, E24, E28 and E30 vehicles.
With the introduction of the E32 in 1988 and the E34 in
1989, electronic coding plugs were utilized in the instrument
cluster.

The change to an electronic coding plug which allowed market specific data to be
assigned to the instrument cluster also contained Non-Volatile Random Access Memory
(NV-RAM), which provided an ability to retain vehicle specific data in the plug such as:

• Vehicle Identification Number

• Accumulated Mileage

• Service Indicator Information

• Coding plug number

• Fuel Tank Size data

• Etc, Etc.

By using a plug that is able to store data, the
instrument cluster can be replaced without
loosing vehicle mileage, unless the coding
plug is damaged.

With the introduction of vehicles like the E31 and E38 the instrument cluster no longer
utilizes a coding plug since it receives most of its input signals directly from a control
module, EKM (E31) or IKE (E38), this allows vehicle data to be directly stored in the con-
trol module and the instrument cluster is no longer coded.  For these vehicles and newer
models, market specific data is stored in the control module (EKM or IKE).  By coding
these modules by way of ZCS coding (refer to ZCS coding) market specific data is
assigned/released to the control module.

Coding Plug Identification

Each coding plug features a stored 5-digit numerical code
that varies between model/equipment, etc.

The code can be read out through the instrument cluster
display by pressing the odometer reset button and turning
the ignition switch to KL R.  The coding plug number will be
display in the instrument cluster matrix.

Ah, the classic “E36 died after a bump, cranks but no fuel, and now half the car talks to nothing” problem. Let’s break this down logically based on symptoms, and then I’ll give you a few tactical places to check.

---

### **Symptoms Recap:**

1. **E36 Convertible.**
2. **Hit a big pothole** → car died instantly.
3. **Cranks fine** → EWS is probably OK.
4. **Fuel pump not priming.**
5. **All fuses/relays checked and confirmed OK.**
6. **OBD under-hood port lights up with dongle/DCAN cable,** but **no comms to phone/laptop.**
7. **OBD tools work fine on E90** → Tools not the issue.
8. No other clear electrical faults — dash may power up, lights OK.

---

### ✅ **What We Know About E36 Electrical Layout:**
- Fuel pump relay is controlled by the **DME** (ECU).
- DME powers up via **main relay**, which in turn is powered through **ignition switch and fusible links**.
- **OBD communication** for E36 uses **pin 20 for TX and 17 for RX**, and requires a powered DME.
- A **crank/no start with no fuel and no OBD comms** strongly suggests the **DME is not alive**.

---

## 🔍 Likely Suspects After a Shock Event

### 🔌 1. **Loose or broken DME connector**
- Located under the hood (passenger side, behind a cover).
- **Check for water intrusion or popped connector.** It might’ve shifted loose from the pothole impact.

### 🧠 2. **DME not powering on**
- If the DME doesn’t get power, it won’t trigger the fuel pump **or respond to diagnostics.**
- **Check DME relay (aka Main Relay)** in the E-box (electrical box under hood).
  - Try **swapping** it with another known good relay.
- **Check for 12V at pin 18 (Red) and pin 27 (Black/Yellow) on the DME connector.**

### 🧨 3. **Blown fusible link**
- VERY COMMON with shock events (rear battery cars like convertibles especially).
- Located **near the battery, under the rear seat**, inline between battery and front of car.
- Often looks good at a glance but is cracked inside — test with a **voltmeter both sides**.

### 🧿 4. **Ignition switch failure or bounce**
- If internal ignition switch contacts fail or bounce from the impact, you may lose switched 12V to DME.
- Check **pin 21 (Green wire)** on the DME harness for switched 12V with ignition ON.

### 🧯 5. **Grounds**
- There are **DME and chassis grounds** under the hood on the strut tower and behind glove box.
- Check for a **broken or loose ground wire** (common with hard jolts).

---

### ❌ Why You Get Power to OBD Dongle But No Communication:
- The **OBD port gets power from fuse F31** (interior fuse box).
- It will light up even if the DME is completely dead or disconnected.
- The **actual communication (TX/RX)** runs from the **DME**, so no DME = no OBD.

---

## 🧰 Quick Test Plan (in order):

1. **Pop DME box open** and reseat all connectors.
2. **Check fuel pump fuse again and power at pump** with key ON (using multimeter or test light).
3. **Swap DME main relay**.
4. **Test fusible link** under rear seat with multimeter – voltage both sides.
5. **Check for power at DME pins** as described above.
6. **Test for ground at DME connector** (especially pin 19 or 24 depending on your DME).

---

### 🔚 If All Else Fails:
If power and ground are present and the DME still doesn’t talk or prime fuel:
- **DME may have cracked or shorted internally** from shock.
- You may need to **test with another known-good DME.**
  - If EWS is still synced and you're just missing fuel, you can do a temporary bridge at the fuel pump relay to see if it fires and runs.

---

### Bonus: Temporary Fuel Relay Bypass
To get it to prime for testing:
1. Pull the fuel pump relay.
2. Bridge **pin 30 to 87** in the socket (check diagram on relay).
3. If pump runs and engine starts, DME isn’t triggering it = dead or unpowered DME.

---

## 🔐 **EWS-II (1995+ E36)** — How It Interacts:

### 💡 **EWS can still allow cranking but kill DME functions**:
- The **starter is triggered directly by EWS**, **not** the DME.
- If EWS **doesn’t send the "OK to run" signal to the DME**, the DME **won’t activate fuel or spark**, but **starter will still turn**.

- **OBD tools get power, but no communication** → DME isn’t even online, which goes beyond EWS.
- **Fuel pump isn’t even priming**, and that’s something the DME controls regardless of EWS status (it primes before cranking).

💥 This all points **not to EWS**, but to the **DME not powering up at all** — because:
- Even if EWS blocks fuel/spark, the DME should still respond over OBD.
- The EWS-DME handshake happens **after** DME boots. If DME doesn’t boot, EWS handshake never occurs.

| Happened after pothole   | Mechanical shock → loose plug, fusible link |

3. **12V at DME pins** — confirm it’s even powered.
4. **Ground at DME and chassis**.
5. If all above is good → suspect **fried DME** from shock or surge.

- This one **kills starter too**.

## 🔒 YES — The OEM Alpine Alarm *Can* Prevent Starting

The **Alpine alarm** (factory accessory or dealer-installed system) integrates **between key ignition, starter, DME power circuits**, and sometimes **fuel pump relay** — depending on how it was installed.

And if it’s **disconnected improperly**, it can absolutely:
- Prevent **fuel pump activation** ✅  
- Cut **power to DME** ✅  
- Block **OBD comms** (if DME doesn’t power up) ✅  
- Still allow **cranking** ❗️✅ *(on E36, starter signal is often direct)*

---

### 🔌 How It Works:
The Alpine system usually installs a black control box **under the driver’s kick panel** or **behind glove box**, and it interrupts one or more of these:
- **Fuel pump relay trigger wire**
- **DME main power**
- **Ignition power (KL15) routing**
- **Starter solenoid (on some models)**

If you just unplug it or it loses power, its **normally open relays stay open**, which = dead car.

## ⚡️ Why Your OBD Port Powered the Dongle — Even With a Dead DME:

The **OBD port on an E36 gets its power from fuse F31 (interior fuse panel)**, which is a general **accessory power source (KL30 or KL15)** — **not directly tied to the DME power circuit**.

So even if your:
- DME is totally dead,
- DME relay is bad,
- Fusible link is blown,
- Alpine alarm is cutting DME power…

💡 **You will still get 12V on pin 16** of the OBD port.

---

## 📡 But… That’s Just Power. Not Communication.

- **Pin 16** on the OBD port = constant +12V (from fuse F31, not DME).
- **Pin 4** = chassis ground.
- **Pin 20** = TX (data output from DME).
- **Pin 17** = RX (data input to DME).

So:

| Signal     | Purpose             | Source       | Status in Your Case        |
|------------|---------------------|--------------|-----------------------------|
| Pin 16     | +12V power          | Fuse F31     | ✅ Still present            |
| Pin 4      | Ground              | Chassis      | ✅ Still present            |
| Pin 20     | TX (DME → scanner)  | DME          | ❌ Dead (DME not powered)   |
| Pin 17     | RX (scanner → DME)  | DME          | ❌ Dead (DME not powered)   |

That’s why your **dongle lights up**, but **can’t talk to anything**.

---

## 🧪 How to Confirm This:
You can take a multimeter and test:
- **Pin 16 (OBD port)** to chassis ground = should read +12V ✅
- **Pin 20 or 17** = may show floating voltage or nothing if DME is unpowered ❌

---

## 🧠 Bottom Line:

> Just because your OBD dongle gets power doesn’t mean the DME is alive.  
> It just means the **fuse for the port is good** — nothing more.

The DME needs:
- Relay power (DME Main Relay),
- 12V on specific pins,
- Ground,
- And no alarm or wiring interruptions.

## 🎯 That Purple Wire: What It Is

You're talking about the **BSD line** — **Bit Serial Data**.

### 🟣 Color:
- It's usually **violet (purple)** or **violet/white** depending on year/engine.
- Found in **N52, N54, N55, and even N20** engines.

---

## 💡 What It Does (BSD Line):
It's a **one-wire digital data bus** used to control and monitor multiple smart components:

| Component               | Controlled/Monitored Over BSD? |
|------------------------|-------------------------------|
| ✅ Electric Water Pump  | Yes                          |
| ✅ Alternator (smart)   | Yes                          |
| ✅ Oil Condition Sensor | Yes                          |
| ✅ Radiator Fan (some)  | Yes                          |
| ✅ IBS (Intelligent Battery Sensor) | Yes *(sometimes via LIN)*

---

## 🔌 Where It Comes From (Source Module):

### ✅ **DME (Digital Motor Electronics)**

> The **DME** is the *master* of the BSD line.

So that purple wire comes **from the DME** (usually pin on connector X60003 or X60004 depending on engine), and runs to:
- The **alternator** (smart regulator)
- The **water pump**
- The **oil level/condition sensor**
- Any other BSD-based devices in your engine bay

---

## ⚠️ What Happens if It Breaks or Shorts?

- No BSD = **all devices on that line go dumb**.
- Water pump will fail-safe → may not run or runs at limp speed.
- Alternator won’t charge properly.
- Oil level sensor won’t report correctly.
- **No fault codes specifically for BSD failure** — just weird faults from all the affected devices.

---

## 🛠 Common Faults You'll See:
- **2E81 / 2E82 / 2E83 / 2E84** – Water pump communication or failure
- **2E8E / 2E8F** – BSD signal missing
- **2E90 / 2E91** – Alternator or LIN/BSD error
- Oil level sensor reports nothing or shows dashes in cluster

---

## 🧪 Quick Test:

1. Unplug **water pump** connector.
2. Look for **violet wire** — test continuity between it and **DME BSD pin**.
3. If open or shorted to ground — there's your issue.

If you reconnect water pump and alternator and everything shares the BSD line, and one of them is shorted internally, it can crash the whole bus.

---

## 🔍 Bonus: DME Connector & BSD Pinouts

**Example for N52/N54 DME:**
- Connector: **X60003** (black), pin **11 or 33** = BSD (varies by engine)
- Wire: **Violet**
- Goes to:
  - Water pump (via big 4-pin plug)
  - Alternator (3-pin plug)
  - Oil level sensor (3-pin)

**Those systems are grounded through the *chassis*** — not the engine.

| Dash lights      | Chassis ground         | ✅ Yes                        |

### ✅ So What Fails If the Ground Strap Is Broken?
- DME can’t ground → no fuel, no spark
- DME doesn’t respond to OBD
- DME won’t trigger fuel pump relay
- Alternator won’t charge (if engine not grounded)
- Other ECU-based stuff dies

**BUT the car still cranks**, because the **starter gets its ground from the block itself**. It doesn’t need the strap to spin.

---

1. Grab a **jumper cable**.
2. Connect one end to **engine block or alternator bracket**.
3. Connect other end to a clean **chassis ground** (strut tower, hood hinge, battery ground post).
4. Try:
   - Key ON — do you hear fuel pump now?
   - Try OBD scanner — any comms?
   - CEL light on dash?

If **anything comes back to life**, your ground strap is toast.

---

## 🔩 Typical E36 Ground Strap Location:
- Bolted between **left engine mount bracket** and **chassis frame rail**, under the car near the subframe.
- Often **corroded**, or ripped during pothole/impact hits.

---

## ✅ Bottom Line:

> The **radio and dash lights are not part of the engine ground path**.  
> Your ground strap can be broken, and all that stuff still works — but **the DME will not**.

If you’ve hit a big pothole, **the strap or its bolts are a prime suspect.**

💯 YEP — the **DME relay** is another **top suspect** in your “crank, no fuel, no OBD” situation, especially after a pothole jolt.

Let’s break it down:

---

## 🔌 What the DME Relay Does:

The **DME Main Relay** powers:
- ✅ The **DME (ECU)** itself
- ✅ The **fuel injectors**
- ✅ The **mass airflow sensor**
- ✅ The **O2 sensors**
- ✅ **OBD communication lines**
- ✅ Triggers the **fuel pump relay** indirectly

> No DME relay = no fuel, no spark, no communication. Exactly your problem.

---

## 🧠 How It Works:
- When you turn the key to **ON**, the **ignition switch sends 12V to the DME**.
- The DME **grounds the DME relay coil**, closing the relay.
- That sends power to all the components above.

---

## 📍 Location:
- In the **E-box under the hood**, passenger side (or driver's side on RHD).
- Inside the black plastic box next to the DME.
- Usually marked “**Motronic**” or it’s a **white relay**, sometimes black or orange.

---

## 🧪 How to Test the DME Relay:

### **Option 1: Swap It**
- Temporarily swap it with another known-good 5-pin relay (like horn or high beams).

### **Option 2: Jumper It**
- Pull the DME relay.
- Jumper **pin 30 to pin 87** with a fused wire. That sends constant power to the DME.

📌 **Pin Layout (Bosch Relay):**
```
   87
  /   \
85     86
  \   /
   30
```

- Pin 30 = Power in (always hot)
- Pin 87 = Output to DME
- Pins 85/86 = Coil

### ➕ What You Should See:
- After jumping: CEL comes on, fuel pump primes, OBD responds.
- If yes → your DME relay is bad or not being triggered.

---

## ⚠️ Common Failure Modes:
- Relay coil opens (vibration can break it)
- Contacts corrode
- Not being grounded by DME due to:
  - No ignition signal
  - Grounding issue
  - Faulty alarm interrupt

---

## 🧠 Pro Tip:
After a pothole, it’s common for:
- DME relay to **physically fail from shock**
- A crusty relay socket to **lose continuity**
- The **ignition switch** to not send power to DME (less likely but possible)

---

## ✅ TL;DR:
> **Bad DME relay = dead DME = no fuel pump, no spark, no OBD.**  
> Cranking still happens because the starter is on a separate circuit.

- **Copper contact plate (rotary cam inside)** — makes contact with forward or reverse terminals

- Put it in forward

- If it suddenly goes → your throw isn’t fully engaging the forward contact

- If the ram extends but **can’t push further**, the pressure spikes and the relief valve goes → “klunk”
- May be low fluid or air in system

- If it **resists or grinds**, you’ve got mechanical interference

- Remove the arm/coupler from the motor shaft

- If the gearbox is stripped: you can open and rebuild (gears are nylon, often cracked)

| Product Type | Works? | Notes |
|--------------|--------|-------|

| ⚫️ **Encapsulators** (POR-15, Eastwood Rust Encapsulator) | ✅ Yes | Designed to **lock in** rust and prevent oxygen/moisture exposure. Needs **solid substrate**, not flakes. |
| 🚿 **Spray-on “rust dissolvers”** (WD-40 Rust Remover, Evapo-Rust spray) | 🟡 Kinda | Works on **light flash rust or small parts**, but not on scale or undercoating. |
| 🧪 **Acid-based removers** (phosphoric acid, naval jelly) | ✅ Yes | Strips rust, but **needs neutralizing**, can damage nearby coatings. Great for small parts. |
| 🔥 **“Rust reformer” spray cans from the parts store** | ❌ Usually trash | Most are thin, barely convert, don’t seal, and flake off. Temporary at best. |

### 1. **Pressure wash + wire brush the spots**
- Get all the dirt, flake, and scale off
- **You want solid metal underneath** before applying anything

### 2. **Treat with converter (Corroseal or Rust-Mort)**
- Brush-on gives better results than spray
- Let it fully cure to black hard surface
- Don’t touch until it’s fully reacted (~24h)

### 3. **Topcoat with a proper sealant**
Two routes:
- 🛡 **POR-15** or **Eastwood Chassis Black** — hard as nails, long-lasting
- 🧰 Or re-coat with **rubberized undercoating** if factory look is important

- In hard-to-reach box sections or seams
- Prevents moisture from creeping in long-term

- ❌ Don’t just spray “rust reformer” and call it a day
- ❌ Don’t coat over loose flake or dirt
- ❌ Don’t trust rubber undercoating to "hide" rust — it traps moisture if compromised

> **Rust is a chemical reaction.** The only way to stop it is:

---

### 🧠 Probable Root Cause of “Klunk”:
If the horizontal motor **klunks** but doesn't move the mechanism:

1. **Plastic gear inside is stripped or cracked**  
   Common with age. Replacements exist (e.g. aluminum or brass upgrades).
   
2. **Cable is frayed or stripped at the gearhead**  
   If it **jumps** but doesn't pull, that’s your sign.

3. **Motor mount bushing cracked**  
   Causes misalignment → internal gear jump → loud clunk.

4. **One of the microswitches (limit switches)** is out of sync  
   Then the control module may be pulsing the motor but hitting a mechanical stop.

---

### 💡 Pro Tip from Vert Vets:
If you disconnect the top motors and unlatch manually, you can **resynchronize the system** like this:

#### Reset Top System:
1. Manually move the top and lid into the **fully closed position**  
2. Open trunk, access the **convertible top module**
3. Hold **top button down** (open or close) for **10+ seconds** until you hear a relay reset
4. This **resets the internal position tracking**

> 🔄 This is crucial if your system got stuck mid-cycle or you ran the motor out of phase.

You’re right — it's one of the **most hated** jobs on the E36 vert.

- Cables are coiled steel inside nylon sheathing
- Feeding them through the existing guides is a **precision job**
- If not perfectly aligned, **they bind or twist**, causing **motor overload → gear strip**

1. Pull the motor, check gear integrity (they crack and skip)
2. Inspect cable ends — look for:

3. Bench test motor with 12V to confirm torque
4. Replace with **metal gear upgrades** (like Delrin or brass ones from ECS or eBay)
5. Regrease and reinstall **perfectly aligned** — that's key

## 🔁 OEM-Style Cable Replacement (a.k.a. “The Painful Way”)

### 📍 Where They Go:
- The **header latch motor** (above the windshield) is powered by an electric motor that turns **two flex cables**, one for each latch.
- These cables run through channels to gearboxes on each side, which physically lock/unlock the roof to the windshield.

---

### 🛠 Steps to Replace:
1. **Remove the windshield trim / header panel**
   - Carefully pry the trim off — don’t crack it (rare, NLA)
   - Expose the motor and gearbox assembly

2. **Pull motor from housing**
   - You’ll see the two flex cables (like speedo cables) plugged into the motor sides

3. **Release cables at motor and latches**
   - Unclip from motor gear and latch ends
   - May require some disassembly of the header mechanism

4. **Replace cables (greased)** into same paths
   - Must be **pushed in fully**
   - If **not seated** → you’ll strip the new gears instantly

> ❗ The key is: **seating depth and cable alignment are absolutely critical**

---

## 🧠 Why This Sucks:

- The trim is fragile and hard to remove cleanly
- The cable paths are tight and **non-serviceable by design**
- If the latch gearboxes are worn, new cables won’t help
- BMW doesn’t even sell the cables separately anymore — it was a full assembly (when available)

---

## ⚙️ Alternative: **Manual Latch Conversion**

### ✅ Why People Do It:
- Tired of dead motors, stripped cables, or alignment hell
- Want to **ditch the latch motor system entirely**
- Still want the top to be fully powered **after manual unlock**

---

### 🔩 How to Convert:

**Option 1: RC-style shafts and couplers**  
- Replace the flex cables with **rigid shafts or RC-style dogbone shafts**
- Use small **U-joints or hex couplers**
- Drive manually with an Allen wrench or small crank

**Option 2: Manual latch install**
- Install small **flip-style latches** or **DZUS-style clips** where the locks used to be
- Use hood pin-style setups or over-center clamps
- Can make it stealthy and strong

> 🎯 The idea is: you **manually unlatch the roof**, then use the power top for the rest  
> System stays fully functional *except* for the auto-locking

---

### 🧰 What You’ll Need:
- Shaft couplers or U-joints (RC/robotics hardware stores)
- 3–5mm steel shaft stock
- Small knob or crank
- Optional: bracket to hold shaft against original latch gear

✅ **Yes — a bad half shaft (axle) absolutely can cause a grinding noise when turning**, and from your description, that’s a top suspect.

Let’s break this down clearly:

---

## 🎧 Symptoms You Described:

- **Grinding noise on right turns only**
- **Goes away when straightening out**
- **Only happens under load**
- **No consistent vibration or noise when going straight**
- You suspect it’s **not the gearbox** — and you’re right.

---

## 🧠 Likely Causes (in order):

### 🔁 1. **Failing CV joint on a rear half shaft**
- Inner CV joint **binds or grinds under load**, especially when the suspension articulates during cornering
- A bad **left-side axle** will typically grind when turning **right** (because the suspension compresses and rotates that side harder)
- If the grease boot is torn or it’s a cheap rebuilt shaft — even more likely

#### 🔍 Confirm:
- Check for torn CV boots
- Grab the axle and try to twist it while holding the hub — play = wear
- Look for rust-colored dust = dry CV joint

---

### ⚙️ 2. **Wheel bearing starting to go**
- Usually causes more of a **howl or growl**, but can feel like grinding
- Sound gets louder as you load that side in a corner

#### Test:
- Jack up the rear and spin the wheel by hand while listening
- Wiggle top/bottom and side/side — any play = replace

---

### 🔩 3. **Dust shield rubbing**
- Sounds dumb, but if the dust shield behind the brake rotor is **slightly bent**, it can:
  - Rub under body flex
  - Only contact at certain angles (e.g., turning)

---

### ❌ 4. **Gearbox / diff issues?**
- Very unlikely unless the diff is out of fluid or the spider gears are dying
- You’d hear **noise during straight-line driving** or **tight low-speed turns in both directions**
- Not the first place to look

---

## 🧪 Quick Diagnosis Tips:

| Test | Result |
|------|--------|
| Turn right in a **parking lot** slowly | Grinding = inner left CV likely |
| Try **braking** during the turn | If noise changes = could also involve hub |
| Floor it in 2nd on a turn | Clicking/popping = CV joint |
| Jack car, spin axle by hand | Crunchy = bad CV joint |
| Feel for **heat** in the axle after driving | Excess heat = dying bearing or dry CV |

---

## 🛠 Fix Strategy:

If you find the half shaft is bad:
- Replace both rear axles if they’re original or unknown brand
- Use **GKN/Löbro or OEM** — avoid eBay rebuilts
- Torque properly — rear axle bolts are often improperly torqued → noise

---

## ✅ TL;DR:

> Yes — a bad **rear CV joint** on the half shaft can 100% cause **grinding when turning**, especially under load.  
> Sounds like your **left rear axle inner joint** is tired and binding on right-hand corners.

## 🚩 Here's What Sucks About Cheap Axles:

## 🧰 But Can You *Make* a Cheap Axle Work?

2. **Disassemble it completely**

3. **Degrease the joints**, inspect for pitting or sharp edges
4. **Regrease with LiquiMoly or Redline CV2**
5. **Install real OE boots** (BMW, Corteco, GKN) — they'll last 10× longer
6. Use **proper clamps** (Oetiker or BMW-style), not worm clamps

- OR they were so old the grease hardened and seized the CV

> 💡 Always use anti-seize or CV-specific spline grease (Molykote G-n or similar) on the outer spline and torque with a calibrated wrench.

can the oem be rebuilt?

💯 **YES** — **OEM BMW/GKN half shafts are absolutely rebuildable**, and doing so is often **the best possible option**, especially if:

- The splines are good (not worn or rusted)
- The shaft itself isn’t twisted or bent
- You're comfortable doing some DIY wrenching and cleanup

---

## 🔧 What Makes OEM Axles Worth Rebuilding?

| Feature | Why It Matters |
|--------|----------------|
| 🛠 Hardened internals (GKN/Löbro) | Lasts longer under heat/load |
| 🧵 Better tolerances | Reduces play and long-term wear |
| 🥇 CV joint design | Smooth articulation, better grease channels |
| ✅ BMW-specific shaft dimensions | No weird preload or spline depth issues |

> Rebuilding OEM axles gives you **better quality than most new aftermarket units**, especially if you use **premium grease + boots**.

---

## 🧰 Rebuild Process (Step-by-Step)

### 🧽 1. **Remove and inspect**
- Check:
  - Splines (inner & outer)
  - CV races and cages for pitting or cracks
  - Shaft runout (should be straight)

### 🪛 2. **Disassemble CV joints**
- Remove clamps and boots
- Use a pick or screwdriver to pop snap rings
- Slide joints off shaft
- Clean everything in solvent (brake cleaner, ultrasonic bath if you have one)

### ⚙️ 3. **Inspect and polish**
- Minor pitting can sometimes be polished out
- Replace CV joint **if chipped or worn** (can buy new outer or inner joints from GKN or Corteco)

### 🧈 4. **Repack with high-temp CV grease**
- Use quality stuff like:
  - Red Line CV2
  - Liqui Moly LM 47
  - GKN supplied moly grease (if buying their kits)

### 🥾 5. **Install new boots and clamps**
- **OEM-style thermoplastic boots** preferred (GKN, Corteco, SKF)
- Avoid cheap rubber — they split fast
- Use Oetiker or crimp-style CV clamps, not worm-gear clamps

### 🔩 6. **Reinstall with anti-seize on splines + proper torque**

---

## 🧰 Parts You Can Use:

| Part | Source |
|------|--------|
| 🥾 Boots | BMW OE, GKN, Corteco, Rein |
| ⚙️ CV joints | GKN (PN varies by side/model), FCP Euro sometimes stocks them |
| 🧈 Grease | GKN, Red Line, or Liqui Moly |
| 🪛 Clamps | GKN or BMW boot kits usually include them |

---

## ⚠️ Watch Out For:

- Some E36 shafts have **staked-on ends** (rare) — makes rebuilding harder, but still possible
- Don’t mix up **inner and outer joints** — the cages and movement range differ
- If your outer CV has **grooves or hammer damage**, you might want to replace that joint rather than reuse it

---

## ✅ TL;DR:

> **OEM BMW half shafts (GKN/Löbro) are totally rebuildable** — and doing so gives you **better-than-new quality** if done right.  
> Replace the boots, repack with good grease, and clean the joints — or replace just the worn ones.

## 🔁 Basic EZGO Electric Motor Wiring (Standard Series or Older TXT):

| Function | What's Happening |

| 🔄 **Forward** | Controller sends current through motor in one polarity |

- 🔥 **Overheated or internally broken**

| Symptom | Likely Cable Issue |
|---------|--------------------|
| ✅ Reverse works | Forward path is broken |
| ❌ Forward fails | Could be cable *or* switch contact on that side |

### 1. **Check Every High-Current Cable Going to the Motor**
- Especially the **A1, A2, F1, F2** terminals (Series motors)

- With the key off and cart in tow mode (if applicable), gently **wiggle or flex the suspect cable**

- Set DMM to DC volts
- Place one lead at controller side of cable, other at motor side

## 🧠 Quick Breakdown: How the EZGO Series Motor Works

These older electric motors (especially in **Series carts**) have:

| Part | Description | Job |
|------|-------------|-----|
| **Armature winding (A1 ↔ A2)** | Inner spinning coil | Drives rotation |
| **Field winding (F1 ↔ F2)** | Stationary coil | Creates the magnetic field that controls direction & torque |

### 🔁 Reversing Direction:
- Forward: Current flows one way through both windings
- Reverse: Current flows the **opposite direction** through **just the field winding**, not both

So if:
- 🔌 **One field winding leg is damaged**
- 🔥 **The field coil is shorted/open**
- 🔩 **A brush isn't making contact**
- 💀 **One terminal is burnt or internally cracked**

👉 Then you'll **lose only one direction**, or get weak/no movement in that direction.

---

## 🔎 How to Tell if One Winding is Bad:

### 💡 Visual Clues:
- Melted or discolored motor case near F1/F2 or A1/A2
- Loose or rotating terminal studs
- One direction works fine, other doesn’t — **even though solenoid clicks**

### 🧪 Meter Tests (Motor unplugged):

#### 🧰 Armature (A1 ↔ A2):
- Test resistance → should read **low (~0.2–0.5Ω)**
- Open = broken winding or disconnected brush

#### 🧰 Field Coils (F1 ↔ F2):
- Should also be **low resistance (~1–2Ω)**
- Open = broken coil or bad internal connection
- Short = you'll see near-zero ohms or very high amperage draw

#### 🧰 Case check (F1 to motor housing):
- Should be **OL (infinite)** — no continuity
- If you get a reading = **winding shorted to case = dead motor**

---

## ✅ TL;DR:

> **Yes, one winding can fail (especially the field winding),** and cause the cart to **only move in one direction**.

It’s rare, but if:
- You rule out cables ✅
- F/R switch is solid ✅
- Controller is sending signal ✅
- And you still get no response in one direction…

💥 Then it’s very likely the **motor’s internal field or armature winding is cooked**.

| Component | What to Check | When to Check |
|-----------|----------------|----------------|
| 🔩 **Brushes** | Wear length, chipping, stuck slides | Every 1–2 years or 250 hrs |
| 🔄 **Commutator** | Pitting, uneven wear, carbon scoring | Every 1–2 years |
| ⚙️ **Bearings** | Noise, slop, drag | If motor is out or after water exposure |
| 🧽 **Vent openings** | Blockage, mud, nests, leaves | Every 6–12 months |
| 🔌 **Terminals** | Tightness, corrosion, melting | Annually, or more in wet/humid climates |
| 🧹 **General clean-out** | Blow out carbon dust, inspect coils | When brushes are serviced |

| Symptom | Likely Cause |
|---------|--------------|
| ⚠️ Only one direction works | Possibly open field winding or bad connection |
| 🔥 Motor gets hot fast | Worn brushes, dragging bearing, high resistance |
| 🎧 Hissing, grinding, or squealing | Dry or bad bearing(s) |
| ⚡ Weak torque or low top speed | Worn brushes or dirty commutator |
| 🚫 Cart stops after a few seconds | Thermal overload or commutator arc fault |

## 🧰 How to Service an EZGO Series Motor (DIY Level)

1. **Disconnect battery pack**
2. **Remove motor from axle**
   - 3 or 4 mounting bolts, depending on model
   - Be careful not to yank wires
3. **Inspect brushes**
   - Slide freely? Cracked or worn short?
   - Still have 1/2" or more? OK
4. **Check commutator**
   - Clean copper surface (light polish with fine emery cloth or Scotch-Brite)
   - No deep pits or burned spots
5. **Check bearings**
   - Spin shaft: any noise or resistance = replace
6. **Blow out with compressed air**
   - Clear carbon dust (don’t use solvents)
7. **Reassemble with anti-seize on mount bolts**

are there forward and reverse brushes?

🔥 Great question — and no, **there are not separate forward and reverse brushes** in EZGO (or really any standard DC series wound golf cart motor).

> ✅ **The brushes are shared for both forward and reverse** — it’s the *direction of current flow* that changes, **not which brushes are used**.

---

## 🧠 Here's How It Works:

### In a standard **series-wound DC motor** (like most EZGO carts):
- You have **4 brushes** (sometimes 2 or 6, depending on design)
- They're evenly spaced around the **commutator**
- The **field windings** and **armature windings** are in series
- The **direction** the motor spins is controlled by **flipping the polarity of current** in **either** the:
  - Field winding (F1/F2), or
  - Armature winding (A1/A2)
  - (but **not both at the same time**, or it cancels out)

### 🔁 Forward vs. Reverse:
| Direction | What Changes | Brushes Used |
|-----------|--------------|---------------|
| 🔄 Forward | Current flows normally through F and A | All brushes used |
| 🔃 Reverse | Current polarity flipped in field | **Same brushes**, just reversed current direction |

> The brushes don't know or care what direction the motor is spinning — they just pass power to the commutator.

---

## 🧰 What Can Still Go Wrong with Brushes (One Direction Only):

Even though the brushes are shared, a **problem with the brush seating or wear** can sometimes affect one direction more than another, due to:
- Uneven wear
- Broken or jammed spring
- A brush only making good contact in one polarity of rotation
- Commutator segment damage that aligns with brush path *only during forward rotation*

---

## ✅ TL;DR:

> **No**, there aren’t forward/reverse-specific brushes.  
The **same brushes serve both directions** — it’s the **current direction** that changes, not the hardware path.

---

If forward doesn’t work but reverse does:
- You likely have a problem with **cabling**, **connections**, or **internal field coil damage**
- Or **a mechanical issue** like a stuck brush, but not a directional one

- A loose or corroded cable can:
  - Pass current briefly
  - **Heat up rapidly**
  - **Increase resistance to the point of cutoff**

> 🔧 **Test**: Do a **live voltage drop test** across each high-current cable during startup  
> 🔥 Feel the terminals — if one gets hot fast, it’s failing under load

---

### 3. 🕹️ **F/R Switch Arcing or Intermittent Contact**
- Manual F/R switches wear inside
- Can cause:
  - Brief contact
  - Arcing
  - Then loss of power
- Especially common if reverse works *just barely*, then cuts out

> 🔧 **Test**: Open the switch, inspect copper pads, and test continuity **under load** (not just static ohms)

---

### 4. 🧠 **Controller Issue (if DCS or PDS model)**
- If you're running a **DCS** or **PDS** cart:
  - The controller uses internal logic for F/R
  - A **partial failure** or **overheat condition** can cause it to drop reverse
  - Forward may already be dead due to internal failure

> 🔧 **Test**: Use a **handheld EZGO diagnostic tool**, or check controller lights/codes (if present)

---

## 🛠️ What to Do Next:

| ✅ Cold Test | Run reverse from stone-cold. Time how long it lasts. |
| 🔌 Cable Check | Inspect all A1/A2/F1/F2 cables — feel them during run |

Great question — and super important for pinpointing **whether your motor windings are good**.

Here are the **expected ohm values** for a typical **EZGO series-wound or DCS motor** (most older 36V/48V carts):

---

## 🔧 **Normal Ohm Values (Motor Disconnected)**

| Test Point | Expected Resistance | What it Means |
|------------|---------------------|----------------|
| **A1 ↔ A2** (Armature) | **~0.2 to 0.5 Ω** | Low resistance = armature coil is good |
| **F1 ↔ F2** (Field winding) | **~1 to 2 Ω** | Slightly higher = longer field coil winding |
| **A1 or F1 to motor case** (Ground) | **OL (infinite)** | **No continuity** — if you get a reading, coil is shorted to case (bad) |

> 📏 Always use a **digital multimeter in ohms mode**, and **zero out the meter first** (touch the leads together — should read 0.0–0.1Ω).

---

## 🧠 What Bad Readings Might Look Like:

| Reading | Problem |
|---------|---------|
| **Open / OL** on A1 ↔ A2 or F1 ↔ F2 | Broken winding, internal disconnect |
| **>2.5–3Ω on F1 ↔ F2** | Corrosion, heat damage, or partial open |
| **~0Ω on F1 ↔ F2** | Shorted field coil (internal short circuit) |
| **Continuity to case** | Coil or terminal shorted to motor housing (dead motor) |

---

## 🧪 Bonus Tip — Test Cold *and* After It Acts Up

If reverse **works briefly then dies**, it could be a **heat-sensitive fault** in the windings.

> Test ohms **cold**, then run it in reverse until it dies. Immediately disconnect the motor and **test again while hot**.

If values jump (open circuit, wildly high, or fluctuating), you've found your culprit.

---

## ✅ TL;DR:

| Test | Good Reading |
|------|--------------|
| **A1 ↔ A2** | ~0.2–0.5Ω |
| **F1 ↔ F2** | ~1–2Ω |
| **Any terminal ↔ case** | OL (no continuity) |

If your readings fall outside that, the motor’s got issues. If the values check out, next stop is the **F/R switch** or **controller/cabling**.

## 🧠 Interpretation: You’re Likely Looking at a **Controller Issue or Motor Field Fault**

The controller **depends on clean feedback from the motor field winding (F1/F2)** to complete the circuit and output full pack voltage on M+.

### So if:
- 🧲 The **field coil is failing or open intermittently**
- 🔌 Or a **bad connection** at F1/F2 breaks the field path
- 🧠 The **controller will NOT send power to M+**

> ✅ This explains:
> - **Why it worked briefly** (good connection/coil)
> - **Why flipping to forward stops everything**
> - **Why even reverse stops working after** (controller faults out or goes into protection)

---

## 🔧 Here’s What You Should Do Next (Exact Steps):

### 1. 🔌 **Check Field Circuit (F1 ↔ F2)**

- Disconnect motor from controller
- Measure resistance **between F1 and F2**
- Should be **~1–2Ω**
- If it's **open**, **very high**, or **drifting after it's been energized**, then the field coil is bad → **motor needs repair/replacement**

---

### 2. 🔧 **Check for Continuity to Case**
- With all motor wires disconnected:
  - Test **F1 → motor housing**
  - Test **A1 → motor housing**
- Both should read **OL (no continuity)**
- If **any** show continuity, motor has an internal short — causes controller protection fault

---

### 3. ⚠️ **Recheck All Motor Cable Lugs**
- Pull and inspect the F1/F2 terminals **for corrosion or green oxide**
- Clean thoroughly — even a flaky or high-resistance field lug can trip the controller

---

### 4. 💡 **Test Controller Field Output**
- Put DMM across **F1 and F2** at the controller (cart powered up, key on, pedal pressed in forward)
- You should see **36V or pulsed voltage**
- If you see **0V**, the controller is not energizing the field = **likely due to open/failed field winding**

---

## 🧠 Why This Happens:

Controllers have **field sensing**:
- If they don’t see a valid circuit through F1/F2, they will NOT output M+ voltage
- That’s why you get nothing in forward
- And when the field gets flakey enough, even reverse stops working

---

## ✅ TL;DR:

> Your **controller won’t output full power unless the field coil (F1/F2) is healthy** and properly connected.  
> The fact that you saw 36V briefly, then nothing, and now even reverse is dead = classic sign of:
- 🔌 A **bad field winding or connection**
- 🧠 A **controller faulting out to protect itself**

ok do power stearing pumps wear out i know that sounds dumb, its super loud i have to check the levels but is it a it works or dont part

Not a dumb question at all — **yes, power steering pumps *absolutely* wear out**, and they don’t always just fail all at once. They can get:

- ✅ Loud  
- ❌ Weak  
- 🩸 Leaky  
- 🧨 Internally damaged  

…and still **“work” enough to steer**, just **noisily or with reduced assist**.

---

## 🧠 Here's How Power Steering Pumps Fail:

| Symptom | What’s Failing | Notes |
|--------|----------------|-------|
| 🔊 **Loud whining/groaning** | Cavitation or worn vanes | Low fluid, air in system, or worn pump |
| 🔄 **Steering is slow or stiff when cold** | Worn internals / low pressure | Common in older E36/E90 LF-20 or LF-30 pumps |
| 💦 **Leaking at front seal** | Shaft seal failure | Often leaks onto belt or alternator |
| 🧪 **Metal shavings in reservoir** | Pump is eating itself | Immediate replacement needed |
| 🎛️ **Steering assist cuts in/out** | Valve body or pressure regulator issue | Seen in pumps with 150k+ miles |

---

## 🔍 Diagnostics Checklist:

### 1. ✅ **Check Fluid First**
- Use **ATF** for most BMWs (not CHF unless specifically labeled)
- Level must be checked **engine OFF** → then cycle steering → check again
- Fluid should be **dark red or light brown**, not black or sparkly

### 2. 🔊 **Listen While Turning at Idle**
- Whining sound = **air, low fluid, or worn vanes**
- Groaning/grinding = **severe wear or cavitation**

### 3. 💨 **Look for Bubbles or Foam**
- Bubbles in the reservoir = **air in system**
- May require **bleeding** (turn wheel full lock side to side with engine running)

### 4. 🧲 **Check for Belt Slip**
- If belt is loose or oily → pump won’t run properly
- Listen for chirp/squeal when steering

---

## 🔧 So: Is It a “Works or Doesn’t” Part?

> ❌ **Nope** — power steering pumps can partially fail, and most do it **gradually**:
- First it gets **a little noisy**
- Then assist becomes **inconsistent**
- Then it starts **leaking**
- Eventually it dies, often taking the **rack seals** or **alternator** with it

---

## 🧰 If It's Super Loud:

| What to Do | Why |
|------------|-----|
| 🔍 Check fluid level and bleed | First, cheapest fix |
| 🛢️ Flush system | If fluid is black or gritty |
| 🔩 Check pulley wobble | Shaft play = pump death |
| 🧯 Replace with OEM or quality reman (ZF or Luk) | If it’s howling, don’t wait too long — it *will* take something else out

---

## ✅ TL;DR:

> Yes, power steering pumps **do wear out**, and they don’t have to totally fail to start causing problems.  
> Loud pump = check fluid **now**, bleed the system, and prepare to replace if noise continues — especially if the car feels sluggish or whines on cold start.
